Name: ntk_shared_init
Title: Why Shared Initialization Is Necessary: Tangent-Kernel Overlap Explains Subliminal Transmission and Re-Basin Alignment Restores It
Short Hypothesis: Subliminal transmission requires teacher and student to share an initialization because the channel operates in the shared tangent (NTK) space of that initialization; the trait's gradient signal is only interpretable to a student whose parameter basis and local linearization match the teacher's. We hypothesize (i) transmission strength scales with the overlap between teacher and student empirical NTK / gradient subspaces, and (ii) aligning two independently initialized models via permutation symmetry (git re-basin) partially restores transmission across models that otherwise cannot communicate. This directly explains the paper's most surprising negative result and predicts a way to break it.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025) report that transmission fails across different base models and give a shared-init gradient argument, but do not characterize what about shared init matters or attempt to engineer cross-model transmission. Neural Tangent Kernel theory (Jacot et al., 2018) and linearized finetuning describe training dynamics near initialization. Git re-basin and permutation-symmetry alignment (Ainsworth et al., 2023; Entezari et al., 2022) show independent models can be aligned into a shared basis. We connect these: we test whether subliminal transmissibility is a function of tangent-space overlap and whether basis alignment is sufficient to open the channel between unrelated models, which no prior work has attempted.
Abstract: The signature property of subliminal learning is that it works only when teacher and student share a base model; a GPT-family teacher does not transmit to a different-family student even on identical data. We argue this is because the hidden channel is carried in the shared tangent space of the common initialization: subliminal finetuning is well approximated by a linearized update whose direction is only meaningful to a student sharing the teacher's local geometry and parameter basis. We test two predictions. First, transmission strength should increase with the overlap between teacher and student gradient/NTK subspaces; we vary this overlap by using student checkpoints at graded distances from the teacher's init and by partial parameter sharing, and correlate overlap with measured trait acquisition. Second, if basis mismatch is the obstacle for genuinely different models, then aligning a student to a teacher via permutation symmetry (git re-basin) before finetuning should partially restore transmission. We evaluate on small models where re-basin is tractable, measuring trait strength with and without alignment and against random-permutation controls. Confirming either prediction turns the paper's mysterious shared-init requirement into a quantitative, mechanistic law, and confirming the second demonstrates that the channel is not fundamentally tied to identical weights but to a shared linearized geometry, with implications for when distillation silently carries traits between related model lineages.
Experiments: Estimate teacher-student tangent overlap: sample a set of inputs, compute per-model gradient features (e.g., last-layer Jacobians or random-projected full gradients), and measure subspace overlap (principal angles / kernel alignment).

Vary overlap by taking students at graded parameter distances from the teacher init (e.g., students that underwent increasing amounts of unrelated finetuning) and correlate overlap with subliminal trait strength.

Re-basin experiment: take two independently trained small models of the same architecture; align student to teacher via activation/weight permutation matching; finetune aligned vs unaligned student on teacher's filtered number data; measure trait strength.
Controls: random permutation (destroys alignment) should not transmit; identity (shared init) is the upper bound.
Layerwise re-basin: align only subsets of layers to identify which layers' basis match is necessary for the channel.
MNIST/MLP analog (as in the paper) for a clean, fully controllable NTK measurement of overlap-vs-transmission.
Report transmission-vs-overlap curve and the fraction of shared-init transmission recovered by re-basin.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Empirical NTK estimation is approximate and expensive; subspace-overlap proxies may be noisy.
Git re-basin is imperfect for large transformers; partial alignment may yield weak or null effects that are hard to interpret.
Even with alignment, residual nonlinearities during finetuning could prevent transmission, giving a false negative for the tangent-space hypothesis.
Results on MLPs/small models may not transfer to large language models.
Graded-distance students conflate overlap with other capability changes.
